newsitem.title: USA: Under cloud, Clinton will appeal for money.
newsitem.headline: Under cloud, Clinton will appeal for money.

text.p: His Democratic Party reeling in debt, President Clinton will urge big-money donors to raise or give $250,000, a week after he asked a federal agency to outlaw such large, unregulated contributions.

Clinton and Vice President Al Gore were to appear Wednesday night at the Mayflower Hotel at a private dinner of 40 to 50 of the party's best fund-raisers to appeal for their help in retiring a $14.4 million debt plus start filling the campaign warchest for 1998 mid-term congressional elections.
"We've got to press ahead. We've got to deal with some of these financial conditions we face. And we've got to get set for the '98 cycle," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Tuesday.

The donors will be asked to raise or give $250,000, which would seem to be contrary to a new Democratic National Committee policy, made in the wake of the fund-raising scandal, to limit large donations to $100,000 a year.

Democratic officials said the fund-raiser would not violate the cap because it is collecting money under a two-year programme in which individuals could give $100,000 this year, $100,000 next year and raise another $50,000 from other sources.

The fund-raiser comes as a federal investigation proceeds into Democratic money raising from last year's campaign cycle. Clinton has tried to blunt criticism by appealing for campaign finance reform, now stalled in Congress.

In the absence of federal legislation, last week Clinton asked the Federal Election Commission to issue a regulation outlawing big "soft money" contributions. Republicans insisted only Congress could take such an action.

Under current rules, wealthy donors, corporations and labour unions can get around federal limits of $1,000 to individual candidates by donating as much money as they want to the Republican or Democratic parties.
The White House said it did not expect the FEC to act on the request for the rest of this year.

"We hope they would. We wish they would. But it's not going to happen. We're still going to have to have a competitive 1998 campaign. We're not going to unilaterally concede the 1998 election to the Republican Party. I'll make that announcement right now," McCurry said.
The party that holds the White House, in this case the Democrats, traditionally loses congressional seats in mid-term elections. Republicans already control both houses of Congress.
At a contentious daily news briefing, McCurry scolded reporters for playing a game of "gotcha" each time Clinton goes to a fund-raiser.
"As long as we're going to have politics and campaigns in this country paid for by private sources, we're going to have to have fund-raisers. Okay? That's just not going to change," he said.

Initially McCurry announced Clinton's appearance at the dinner would be closed to reporters because he would be discussing campaign strategy and did not want Republicans to find out about Democratic campaign plans for 1998.
Later he said Clinton's opening remarks would be available to the press.
